etymology: Old English forst, from freeze. Frost is water made visible by cold — the same substance, hardened.
biblical_def: Frost is freezing cold and its white deposit. Jacob names it as the cost of twenty years' service: “in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep departed from mine eyes” (Gen 31:40). God asks Job who fathered it: “the hoary frost of heaven, who hath gendered it?” (Job 38:29). The psalmist files it among the acts of a sovereign hand: “He giveth snow like wool: he scattereth the hoarfrost like ashes” (Psa 147:16), and the manna appeared “as small as the hoar frost on the ground” (Exo 16:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines frost as that state or temperature of the air which occasions freezing; and the fine particles of ice formed by the congelation of dew or vapor.
webster_full: FROST, n. A fluid state of the air which occasions freezing or the congelation of water.
2. The act of freezing; congelation of fluids.
3. Frozen dew; called also hoar frost.
scriptures: Thus I was; in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep departed from mine eyes.
Out of whose womb came the ice? and the hoary frost of heaven, who hath gendered it?
He giveth snow like wool: he scattereth the hoarfrost like ashes.
And when the dew that lay was gone up, behold, upon the face of the wilderness there lay a small round thing, as small as the hoar frost on the ground.
corruption_summary: Weather is treated as the one region of life where God is not personally active, so believers thank Him for outcomes and never for the mechanism.
corruption_paragraphs: Job 38 spends its longest section on weather precisely because it is the realm men least control and least credit. Hath the rain a father? or who hath begotten the drops of dew? Out of whose womb came the ice? and the hoary frost of heaven, who hath gendered it? The questions are not meteorological but paternal, and they are unanswerable by a man who has just spent thirty chapters explaining the universe.

Exodus 16:14 makes the frost an image of provision. When the dew was gone up, there lay a small round thing, as small as the hoar frost on the ground — manna described by comparison to the least impressive thing in a cold morning. God's daily supply arrived looking like frost, which is to say looking like nothing, and had to be gathered before the sun rose high.
roots_summary: Hebrew qerach (H7140), ice or frost; kephor (H3713), hoarfrost, from a root meaning to cover.
roots_lines: Hebrew qerach (H7140) — frost, ice; Genesis 31:40, Job 37:10, by the breath of God frost is given.
Hebrew kephor (H3713) — hoarfrost; Exodus 16:14, Psalm 147:16, Job 38:29.
Hebrew sheleg (H7950) — snow; the companion of frost in Psalm 147:16.
usage: “The drought consumed me, and the frost by night” — Jacob's twenty years priced.
“The hoary frost of heaven, who hath gendered it?” — a paternal question, not a scientific one.
“As small as the hoar frost on the ground” — provision that looked like nothing.

pos: n. pl. (frozen missiles from heaven; rendering Hebrew eben barad)
etymology: Hail with stone — the translators' compound for hail that behaves as ammunition rather than weather.
biblical_def: Hailstones are hail large enough to kill. At Beth-horon the LORD “cast down great stones from heaven upon them… they were more which died with hailstones than they whom the children of Israel slew with the sword” (Jos 10:11). The seventh plague brought hail mingled with fire (Exo 9:24). Job is asked whether he has seen the treasures of the hail, “which I have reserved against the time of trouble, against the day of battle and war” (Job 38:22–23), and Revelation ends with a hail of great weight (Rev 16:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hail as masses of ice or frozen vapor, falling from the clouds in showers or storms; and a hailstone as a single mass of ice falling from a cloud.
webster_full: HAIL, n. Masses or particles of ice, or frozen vapor, falling from the clouds in showers or storms.
HAILSTONE, n. A single mass of ice falling from a cloud.
scriptures: And it came to pass, as they fled from before Israel, and were in the going down to Bethhoron, that the LORD cast down great stones from heaven upon them unto Azekah, and they died: they were more which died with hailstones than they whom the children of Israel slew with the sword.
Exo 9:24
So there was hail, and fire mingled with the hail, very grievous, such as there was none like it in all the land of Egypt since it became a nation.
Hast thou entered into the treasures of the snow? or hast thou seen the treasures of the hail,
And there fell upon men a great hail out of heaven, every stone about the weight of a talent: and men blasphemed God because of the plague of the hail; for the plague thereof was exceeding great.
corruption_summary: A God who arms the weather is quietly filed under primitive religion, and with Him goes any serious doctrine of judgment inside history.
corruption_paragraphs: Joshua 10:11 makes an accounting note that is easy to skim: they were more which died with hailstones than they whom the children of Israel slew with the sword. On Israel's most famous day of victory, the majority of enemy casualties were not inflicted by Israel at all. The battle was genuinely fought, the men genuinely swung swords, and the decisive blow came from a sky they did not command.

Job 38:22 supplies the doctrine underneath: God speaks of the treasures of the hail, reserved against the time of trouble, against the day of battle and war. Weather is described as an armoury with stock kept in reserve. That is a hard idea for a culture that has learned to read every storm as a system and nothing more — but it is the settled assumption of Scripture, and it makes both judgment and deliverance historical rather than merely spiritual.
roots_summary: Hebrew barad (H1259), hail; joined with eben (H68), stone, to make the compound of Joshua 10:11 and Ezekiel 13:11.
roots_lines: Hebrew barad (H1259) — hail; Exodus 9:18-26, Job 38:22, Isaiah 28:17.
Hebrew eben (H68) — stone; joined to hail in Joshua 10:11, great stones from heaven.
Greek chalaza (G5464) — hail; Revelation 8:7, 11:19, 16:21.
usage: “More which died with hailstones than… with the sword” — the decisive blow fell from the sky.
“The treasures of the hail… reserved against the day of battle” — weather as armoury.
“Hail mingled with fire” — the seventh plague on Egypt.

pos: n. (a flash from heaven; rendering Hebrew baraq, Greek astrape)
etymology: From lighten, to flash. Scripture's interest is in its speed and its universal visibility — both of which it makes theological.
biblical_def: Lightning is the sudden flash of heaven. Christ uses it for the manner of His return, ruling out any secret or local arrival: “For as the lightning cometh out of the east, and shineth even unto the west; so shall also the coming of the Son of man be” (Mat 24:27). He uses it again for Satan's fall (Luk 10:18). Sinai is described by it (Exo 19:16), the throne in Revelation issues it (Rev 4:5), and the angel at the tomb had a countenance “like lightning” (Mat 28:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lightning as a sudden discharge of electricity from a cloud, or from the earth to a cloud, which produces a vivid flash of light.
webster_full: LIGHTNING, n. A sudden discharge of electricity from a cloud to the earth, or from the earth to a cloud, or from one cloud to another, producing a vivid flash of light.
2. A sudden brightness; as the lightning of the countenance.
scriptures: For as the lightning cometh out of the east, and shineth even unto the west; so shall also the coming of the Son of man be.
And he said unto them, I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven.

And it came to pass on the third day in the morning, that there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud upon the mount, and the voice of the trumpet exceeding loud; so that all the people that was in the camp trembled.
Rev 4:5
And out of the throne proceeded lightnings and thunderings and voices: and there were seven lamps of fire burning before the throne, which are the seven Spirits of God.
corruption_summary: Every private claim that Christ has secretly returned, or is present in one place with one group, is refuted by the single simile He chose — lightning is seen by everyone at once.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 24 sets the simile inside a warning about exactly this error. If they shall say unto you, Behold, he is in the desert; go not forth: behold, he is in the secret chambers; believe it not. For as the lightning cometh out of the east, and shineth even unto the west; so shall also the coming of the Son of man be. The comparison functions as a test: any return that requires an insider to point it out is not the one Christ described.

Luke 10:18 shows the other direction of the flash. I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven — spoken to seventy ordinary disciples returning from a mission, astonished that even the devils were subject to them. The fall was as sudden and as visible from above as the coming will be from below, and Christ's next word keeps them from pride: rejoice not that the spirits are subject unto you, but rather rejoice, because your names are written in heaven.
roots_summary: Hebrew baraq (H1300), lightning, a flash — also used of a glittering sword; Greek astrape (G796), lightning, brightness.
roots_lines: Hebrew baraq (H1300) — lightning; Exodus 19:16, Psalm 97:4, his lightnings enlightened the world.
Greek astrape (G796) — lightning, bright shining; Matthew 24:27, Luke 10:18, 17:24.
Hebrew chaziz (H2385) — a flash, thunderbolt; Job 28:26, a way for the lightning of the thunder.
usage: “As the lightning cometh out of the east, and shineth even unto the west” — nothing secret about it.
“I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven” — the fall was as sudden as the coming.
“His countenance was like lightning” — the angel at the empty tomb.

etymology: From Latin vapor, steam. Scripture's vapour is chiefly a figure for brevity — something with a shape that will not keep it.
biblical_def: A vapour is a mist that shows and vanishes. James makes it the answer to presumptuous planning: “whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away” (Jas 4:14). Job uses the same brevity for consolation and complaint alike, and Proverbs warns that “the getting of treasures by a lying tongue is a vanity tossed to and fro” (Pro 21:6). Acts quotes Joel's promise of “vapour of smoke” before the great and notable day (Act 2:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vapor as an elastic aeriform fluid rendered aeriform by heat; visible steam or fume; and figuratively, something unsubstantial or fleeting.
webster_full: VAPOR, n. In a general sense, an invisible elastic fluid, rendered aeriform by heat.
2. Visible steam or fume; as the vapor of a boiling liquid.
3. Something unsubstantial or fleeting.
scriptures: Jas 4:14
Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.
Act 2:19
And I will shew wonders in heaven above, and signs in the earth beneath; blood, and fire, and vapour of smoke:
Pro 21:6
The getting of treasures by a lying tongue is a vanity tossed to and fro of them that seek death.
Jas 4:15
For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that.
corruption_summary: Planning is treated as either faithless or absolute, when James forbids neither the plan nor the profit — only the sentence that leaves God out of it.
corruption_paragraphs: James 4 is often misread as a rebuke of business. Read it closely and the offence is grammatical: to day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain. Every clause is a settled future stated by a creature who cannot guarantee his own next heartbeat. James does not tell them to stop trading; he tells them to say instead, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that.

The vapour image is chosen for its shape rather than its insignificance. A vapour is genuinely visible, genuinely present, and genuinely gone — not nothing, but nothing that lasts. That is a more useful picture of a human life than either despair or self-importance allows, and it makes the Lord's will the only sensible clause to hang a plan on.
roots_summary: Greek atmis (G822), vapour, mist; Hebrew hebel (H1892), breath, vapour — the vanity of Ecclesiastes is literally a vapour.
roots_lines: Greek atmis (G822) — vapour, mist; James 4:14, Acts 2:19.
Hebrew hebel (H1892) — breath, vapour, vanity; Ecclesiastes 1:2, vanity of vanities.
Greek phainomai (G5316) — to appear; James 4:14, appeareth for a little time.
usage: “It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time” — visible, present, and gone.
“If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this” — the clause that was missing.
“Vapour of smoke” — Joel's sign quoted at Pentecost.

pos: n., adj. (deep red; rendering Hebrew tola and karmil)
etymology: From Arabic qirmiz, the kermes insect from which the dye was made. Crimson is a dye of animal origin, fast and difficult to remove.
biblical_def: Crimson is deep fast red. Isaiah stakes the gospel's boldest promise on the dye's permanence: “Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool” (Isa 1:18). The colour is also the sanctuary's — crimson and its companions clothe the temple's veil (2Ch 3:14) — and Jeremiah uses it of a nation painting itself to attract lovers (Jer 4:30).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines crimson as a deep red color tinged with blue; and as a noun, a deep red color, or red in general.
webster_full: CRIMSON, n. A deep red color; a red slightly tinged with blue; or a beautiful deep red, as the color of arterial blood.
CRIMSON, a. Of a beautiful deep red.
CRIMSON, v.t. To dye with crimson; to make red.
scriptures: Isa 1:18
Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
And he made the vail of blue, and purple, and crimson, and fine linen, and wrought cherubims thereon.
Jer 4:30

And when thou art spoiled, what wilt thou do? Though thou clothest thyself with crimson, though thou deckest thee with ornaments of gold, though thou rentest thy face with painting, in vain shalt thou make thyself fair; thy lovers will despise thee, they will seek thy life.
Rev 7:14
And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 1:18 is quoted as gentle reassurance, when it is a courtroom summons — let us reason together is God calling the guilty to argue the case.
corruption_paragraphs: The force of the promise lies in the chemistry. Crimson and scarlet were fast dyes, made from the crushed kermes insect and driven into the fibre; they were chosen for garments precisely because they would not wash out. Isaiah's audience knew that, which is why the offer is astonishing rather than sentimental: a stain engineered to be permanent will be removed entirely, and the fibre will be as white as wool.

The setting is also worth keeping. Isaiah 1 has just described hands full of blood and feasts God hates, and the invitation to reason together is a legal summons, not a fireside chat. God calls the guilty into court to hear the verdict — and the verdict is acquittal on terms He supplies. Revelation completes the picture with a laundry no one expects: they have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
roots_summary: Hebrew tola (H8438), the crimson worm and its dye; karmil (H3758), crimson; shani (H8144), scarlet.
roots_lines: Hebrew tola (H8438) — worm, crimson; Isaiah 1:18, and Psalm 22:6, I am a worm, and no man.
Hebrew karmil (H3758) — crimson; 2 Chronicles 2:7, 3:14.
Hebrew shani (H8144) — scarlet; the thread of Rahab's window and the tabernacle hangings.
usage: “Though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool” — a fast dye removed entirely.
“Come now, and let us reason together” — a courtroom summons, not a fireside chat.
“Made them white in the blood of the Lamb” — the only laundry that works.

etymology: From Greek krustallos, ice — the ancients believed rock crystal was water frozen so hard it could not thaw. The name preserves the theory.
biblical_def: Crystal is transparent clarity. Scripture reserves it for the architecture of heaven: the firmament over the living creatures is “as the colour of the terrible crystal” (Eze 1:22); before the throne is “a sea of glass like unto crystal” (Rev 4:6); the holy city has light “like a jasper stone, clear as crystal” (Rev 21:11); and the river of water of life is “clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb” (Rev 22:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines crystal as a regular solid body with a smooth surface, to which minerals affect to conform; and a species of glass more perfect in transparency.
webster_full: CRYSTAL, n. In chemistry and mineralogy, an inorganic body which by the operation of affinity has assumed the form of a regular solid, terminated by a certain number of plane and smooth surfaces.
2. A factitious body cast in glass-houses, called crystal glass.
3. A species of glass more perfect in its composition and transparency than common glass.
scriptures: Rev 4:6
And before the throne there was a sea of glass like unto crystal: and in the midst of the throne, and round about the throne, were four beasts full of eyes before and behind.
Having the glory of God: and her light was like unto a stone most precious, even like a jasper stone, clear as crystal;
Rev 22:1
And he shewed me a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb.
Eze 1:22
And the likeness of the firmament upon the heads of the living creature was as the colour of the terrible crystal, stretched forth over their heads above.
corruption_summary: Heaven is imagined as vague and misty, when every description Scripture gives insists on transparency — nothing there is obscured, including us.
corruption_paragraphs: The consistent note in these visions is not brightness but clarity. A sea of glass like unto crystal, a city whose light is clear as crystal, a river clear as crystal — the emphasis falls on the absence of anything cloudy, opaque, or concealed. That is a moral property before it is an aesthetic one: heaven is the place where nothing is hidden, which is glorious for those washed and unbearable for those who are not.

Revelation 22:1 attaches the clarity to a source: a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb. The water is clear because of where it comes from. Nothing upstream is polluting it, which is precisely what cannot be said of any river, institution, or heart in the present world.
roots_summary: Greek krustallos (G2930), rock crystal or ice; krustallizo (G2929), to shine like crystal, used only of the holy city.
roots_lines: Greek krustallos (G2930) — crystal, ice; Revelation 4:6 and 22:1.
Greek krustallizo (G2929) — to be clear as crystal; only Revelation 21:11.
Hebrew qerach (H7140) — ice, crystal; Ezekiel 1:22, the colour of the terrible crystal.
usage: “A sea of glass like unto crystal” — before the throne, nothing cloudy.
“Clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne” — the water is clean at its source.
“The colour of the terrible crystal” — Ezekiel's firmament.

pos: n., v. (a flower, to bloom; rendering Hebrew tsuts and perach)
etymology: Old English blostm, a flower. Blossom is the stage of promise — the visible pledge of fruit not yet formed.
biblical_def: To blossom is to break into flower. Aaron's rod settles a rebellion by doing it overnight: “the rod of Aaron for the house of Levi was budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds” (Num 17:8) — bud, blossom, and ripe fruit at once on dead wood. Isaiah promises that “the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose” (Isa 35:1), and Habakkuk sets his famous confession against its failure: “although the fig tree shall not blossom… yet I will rejoice in the LORD” (Hab 3:17–18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines blossom as the flower of a plant, or the essential organs of fructification; and as a verb, to put forth blossoms or flowers, to bloom, to flower.
webster_full: BLOSSOM, n. The flower of a plant, or the essential organs of reproduction, with their appendages.
BLOSSOM, v.i. To put forth blossoms or flowers; to bloom; to blow; to flower.
2. To flourish and prosper.
scriptures: Num 17:8

And it came to pass, that on the morrow Moses went into the tabernacle of witness; and, behold, the rod of Aaron for the house of Levi was budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds.
Isa 35:1
The wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad for them; and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose.
Hab 3:17

Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls:
Hab 3:18
Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation.
corruption_summary: Faith is measured by visible flourishing, so a barren season is read as divine displeasure — and Habakkuk's whole point is that worship survives the empty branch.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 17 is a lesson about how God settles disputes over authority. Twelve rods were laid up before the LORD overnight, and one came out carrying buds, blossoms, and ripe almonds together — three stages at once on wood that had been cut from the tree. The vindication was not an argument but a resurrection, and the rod was kept in the ark as a permanent answer to the murmurers.

Habakkuk 3 supplies the harder lesson. Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat… yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation. The prophet lists total agricultural collapse — every source of food gone — and then places his joy somewhere the failure cannot reach. Blossom or no blossom, the object of his rejoicing is unchanged.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsuts (H6692), to blossom or flourish; perach (H6525), a bud or flower; both used of Aaron's rod in Numbers 17.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsuts (H6692) — to blossom, flourish; Numbers 17:8, Psalm 92:7, the wicked spring as the grass.
Hebrew perach (H6525) — bud, blossom; the almond blossoms of the golden candlestick, Exodus 25:33.
Hebrew parach (H6524) — to bud, break forth; Isaiah 35:1-2, it shall blossom abundantly.
usage: “Bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds” — three stages at once on dead wood.
“The desert… shall blossom as the rose” — the promise to barren ground.
“Although the fig tree shall not blossom… yet I will rejoice” — worship past the empty branch.

pos: n. pl. (flying embers; rendering Hebrew reshaph and zeq)
etymology: Old English spearca. A spark is fire's smallest unit and its most mobile — the part that travels.
biblical_def: Sparks are flying embers. Eliphaz states the proverb that has outlived his bad counsel: “man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward” (Job 5:7) — trouble is native to human life, as inevitable as the direction embers take. Isaiah warns those who make their own light: “walk in the light of your fire, and in the sparks that ye have kindled. This shall ye have of mine hand; ye shall lie down in sorrow” (Isa 50:11). Leviathan's mouth throws them out (Job 41:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a spark as a small particle of fire or ignited substance, which is emitted from bodies in combustion; and a small transient light.
webster_full: SPARK, n. A small particle of fire or ignited substance, which is emitted from bodies in combustion.
2. A small transient light.
3. A small portion of any thing active.
scriptures: Job 5:7
Yet man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward.

Behold, all ye that kindle a fire, that compass yourselves about with sparks: walk in the light of your fire, and in the sparks that ye have kindled. This shall ye have of mine hand; ye shall lie down in sorrow.
Out of his mouth go burning lamps, and sparks of fire leap out.
Jas 3:5
Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!
corruption_summary: Self-generated light is the default religion of the age — kindle your own fire, find your own way — and Isaiah names both the permission and the outcome.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 50:11 is a chilling verse because God grants the request before pronouncing the consequence. Behold, all ye that kindle a fire, that compass yourselves about with sparks: walk in the light of your fire, and in the sparks that ye have kindled. The permission is real — men may light their own way and live by it. So is the ending: this shall ye have of mine hand; ye shall lie down in sorrow. Self-made light burns exactly as long as the fuel lasts.

Job 5:7 is worth keeping even though Eliphaz was a poor comforter, since Scripture records the saying without endorsing his application. Man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward — trouble is not an interruption of normal life but a property of it. A gospel that promises exemption is arguing with the observed physics of a fallen world; a gospel that promises company in the fire is offering what Scripture actually holds out.
roots_summary: Hebrew reshaph (H7565), a flame or spark, literally sons of flame in Job 5:7; zeq (H2131), a firebrand or spark, in Isaiah 50:11.
roots_lines: Hebrew reshaph (H7565) — flame, spark; Job 5:7, sons of the flame fly upward.
Hebrew zeq (H2131) — spark, firebrand; Isaiah 50:11, the sparks that ye have kindled.
Greek helikos (G2245) — how great; James 3:5, how great a matter a little fire kindleth.
usage: “Man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward” — trouble is native, not exceptional.
“Walk in the light of your fire… ye shall lie down in sorrow” — self-made light, granted and judged.
“How great a matter a little fire kindleth” — James on the tongue.

pos: n. pl. (falls of rain; rendering Hebrew rebibim and geshem)
etymology: Old English scur, a brief fall of rain. A shower is rain in portions — repeated, seasonal, and given rather than taken.
biblical_def: Showers are falls of rain, and Scripture treats them as the standard picture of blessing that must be sent. Ezekiel promises “there shall be showers of blessing” (Eze 34:26). Deuteronomy sets doctrine itself under the figure: “My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew, as the small rain upon the tender herb, and as the showers upon the grass” (Deu 32:2). Jeremiah asks whether any of the vanities of the Gentiles can cause rain, and answers that Israel's hope is in the LORD, “for thou hast made all these things” (Jer 14:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a shower as a fall of rain or hail of short duration; and figuratively, a copious supply bestowed.
webster_full: SHOWER, n. A fall of rain or hail of short duration.
2. A fall of things from the air in thick succession; as a shower of darts.
3. A copious supply bestowed.
scriptures: And I will make them and the places round about my hill a blessing; and I will cause the shower to come down in his season; there shall be showers of blessing.
Deu 32:2
My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew, as the small rain upon the tender herb, and as the showers upon the grass:

Are there any among the vanities of the Gentiles that can cause rain? or can the heavens give showers? art not thou he, O LORD our God? therefore we will wait upon thee: for thou hast made all these things.
Zec 10:1
Ask ye of the LORD rain in the time of the latter rain; so the LORD shall make bright clouds, and give them showers of rain, to every one grass in the field.
corruption_summary: Blessing is treated as something engineered by technique, when Scripture treats rain as the type of everything that must be asked for and cannot be manufactured.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 32:2 is Moses' description of how teaching should land, and every image is meteorological and gentle: my doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew, as the small rain upon the tender herb, and as the showers upon the grass. Nothing there is forced. Doctrine is meant to soak in over time, on tender growth, at a rate the ground can absorb — a rebuke to preaching that arrives as a flood and runs off.

Zechariah 10:1 gives the instruction the church routinely forgets: ask ye of the LORD rain in the time of the latter rain; so the LORD shall make bright clouds, and give them showers of rain. There is a season for asking, and the asking is not optional decoration on top of natural process. Jeremiah's question stands as the alternative — are there any among the vanities of the Gentiles that can cause rain? The honest answer has not changed.
roots_summary: Hebrew rebibim (H7241), copious showers; geshem (H1653), heavy rain; malqosh (H4456), the latter rain of the harvest season.
roots_lines: Hebrew rebibim (H7241) — showers; Deuteronomy 32:2, Psalm 65:10, Micah 5:7.
Hebrew geshem (H1653) — rain, shower; Ezekiel 34:26, showers of blessing.
Hebrew malqosh (H4456) — latter rain; Zechariah 10:1, James 5:7.
usage: “There shall be showers of blessing” — blessing sent, not engineered.
“My doctrine shall drop as the rain” — teaching at a rate the ground absorbs.
“Ask ye of the LORD rain in the time of the latter rain” — there is a season for asking.

pos: n., v. (dust, to grind fine; rendering Hebrew abaq and daq)
etymology: From Latin pulvis, dust. To reduce a thing to powder is to make it irrecoverable — the shape cannot be reassembled.
biblical_def: Powder is matter ground to dust. Moses treats the golden calf with deliberate thoroughness: he “burnt it in the fire, and ground it to powder, and strawed it upon the water, and made the children of Israel drink of it” (Exo 32:20). Josiah does the same to the idols of Judah (2Ki 23:6). Christ applies the image to Himself as the stone: “on whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder” (Mat 21:44), and the Song asks who comes out of the wilderness “perfumed… with all powders of the merchant” (Son 3:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines powder as any dry substance composed of minute particles; and as a verb, to reduce to fine particles, to pulverize, to comminute.
webster_full: POWDER, n. Any dry substance composed of minute particles, as dust, flour, or the like.
POWDER, v.t. To reduce to fine particles; to comminute; to pulverize; to triturate.
2. To sprinkle with powder.
scriptures: And he took the calf which they had made, and burnt it in the fire, and ground it to powder, and strawed it upon the water, and made the children of Israel drink of it.

And he brought out the grove from the house of the LORD, without Jerusalem, unto the brook Kidron, and burned it at the brook Kidron, and stamped it small to powder, and cast the powder thereof upon the graves of the children of the people.
And whosoever shall fall on this stone shall be broken: but on whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder.
Son 3:6
Who is this that cometh out of the wilderness like pillars of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all powders of the merchant?
corruption_summary: Idols today are managed, moderated, or renamed; Moses ground his to powder and made the people drink it, on the principle that a repented sin should be made unrecoverable.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 32:20 is a study in thoroughness. Moses did not confiscate the calf, or store it, or melt it back into usable gold. He burned it, ground it to powder, scattered it on the water, and made the people drink the water — so that the idol passed through them and out, and no fragment remained that could be reassembled or quietly retained. Repentance that leaves the material intact is negotiation.

Matthew 21:44 turns the image toward the person of Christ, and the sentence has two halves that cover everyone: whosoever shall fall on this stone shall be broken; but on whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder. There is a breaking that a man chooses by falling on the stone in repentance, and a grinding that falls on him. Nobody in the sentence remains unbroken; the only question is which encounter he has.
roots_summary: Hebrew abaq (H80), fine dust; daq (H1854), to crush small; Greek likmao (G3039), to winnow or grind to powder.
roots_lines: Hebrew daq (H1854) — to crush, beat small; Exodus 32:20, 2 Kings 23:6, ground it to powder.
Hebrew abaq (H80) — fine dust, powder; Song of Solomon 3:6, powders of the merchant.
Greek likmao (G3039) — to grind to powder, scatter as chaff; Matthew 21:44, Luke 20:18.
usage: “Ground it to powder, and strawed it upon the water” — an idol made unrecoverable.
“On whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder” — the stone nobody escapes.
“All powders of the merchant” — the same word for costly fragrance.
